attribution.note: Marcus quotes his own earlier essay and calls the view his 'longstanding position', so he endorses it. The claim scored is his position, not the claim that Altman echoed it.

semantics.note: 'Would not be enough' is firm, unhedged language about what current techniques can reach. The qualifier 'alone' is kept. No deadline was given.

contract.note: The plain readings of 'current techniques' (the 2023–24 LLM scaling approaches) and 'AGI' (human-level general capability) are ordinary. The two-sided early-resolution rule is fair, and continued non-achievement correctly settles nothing.

evidence.note: A Sept 2026 assessment says no accepted AGI test exists and that GPT-6 Astra is not established as AGI. It gives no impossibility result and no verified AGI.
Independent ARC-AGI-3 results show strong progress, but ARC itself says this does not establish AGI. It also does not show which methods were used.

reviews.rationale: This is an undated forecast that current techniques alone will not reach AGI. The packet has no independently verified AGI built only with those techniques, and no accepted result showing they are insufficient. Astra's progress is material but is explicitly not AGI. Neither resolution condition is met by the cutoff.

attribution.note: Marcus describes his own caution that LLMs aren't really AGI and stands by it in the post.

semantics.note: A present-tense, firm claim about the LLMs of launch day, including o1. The normalised proposition matches it.

contract.note: The result depends on what AGI means, but the plain reading (broadly human-level general capability, not perfection) is ordinary and fair. Under it, the claim is scored.

evidence.note: OpenAI's launch-era system card is a company disclosure, but it reports its own model failing agentic lab tasks and says models cannot yet automate them. A company admitting gaps in its own model is credible.

Independent ARC Prize test one day after launch: o1-preview scored about 18–21%, adapted poorly to novel tasks, and ARC says new ideas are still needed for AGI. The contract counts launch-era evaluations.
A preprint reports broad strengths but describes 'progress towards' AGI, not AGI achieved. It is a counterweight, not a contradiction.

reviews.rationale: Launch-era evidence shows large gaps in adapting to novel tasks (ARC) and in agentic task execution (system card). These do not fit broadly human-level general capability. Even the most favourable evaluation (e5) calls o1-preview progress toward AGI, not AGI. On the plain reading, the claim holds for Sept 12, 2024.

attribution.note: These are Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: The drafter kept 'appears'. That word is a hedge on how confident Marcus is, so the statement is a tentative impression rather than a firm assertion.

contract.note: The contract admits 'appears' signals uncertainty but still scores the claim on a plain reading. Policy allows plain-reading scoring only for firm language, so scoring this hedge is not fair to the speaker.

evidence.note: OpenAI's launch post discloses reinforcement-learning training but says nothing about how much synthetic data was used.
OpenAI's paper confirms model-generated data in o1-preview's safety training. That covers only one stage, not heavy reliance overall.
ARC Prize's contemporary analysis infers synthetic chain-of-thought training but admits it knows few training details.

reviews.rationale: 'Appears to depend heavily' is hedged, a tentative impression rather than a firm claim, so policy says it is not scored. Even if it were scored, the packet confirms some synthetic data (in safety training) but cannot establish heavy reliance.

attribution.note: Marcus makes the comparison himself. The quoted description of o1 is correctly credited to Altman.

semantics.note: A claim that two dated statements match. 'Almost exactly' is preserved, and the difference between GPT-4 and o1 is noted.

contract.note: Comparing the substance of the two statements rather than requiring identical wording is fair. The contract also correctly avoids treating this as proof that the GPT-4 predictions came true.

evidence.note: Marcus's Dec 25, 2022 post is the record of the original prediction: GPT-4 will seem smarter, initial buzz will give way to scrutiny, and many problems will remain. As his own text, it cannot prove the match by itself.
Altman's Sept 12, 2024 post exists and contains all three elements: still flawed, still limited, and more impressive on first use than later. Marcus's paraphrase of it is accurate.

reviews.rationale: The 2022 prediction expected persistent problems, an initial impression that would fade, and many problems remaining. Altman's 2024 post makes the same three points about o1. The models differ, and Marcus framed the fading impression as scientific scrutiny while Altman framed it as user experience, but on substance 'almost exactly' is a fair description.
